articles.title: What is this?
articles.body:
# Human-Agent Collaboration on Structured Data
Today, the formats we use for structured data leave a gap:

-  **CSV** is not expressive enough.
-  **JSON** is hard for humans to navigate and edit.
-  **Excel (XLSX)** is cumbersome for agents to navigate and edit.

JSON Views closes that gap with an editor that makes JSON files look like a **Notion database**. People can browse records, open pages, and edit fields while agents work with the same underlying JSON.

A small **`$jsonviews`** property inside the file holds the column schema and saved views of its important parts. Users can jump straight to the useful tables and pages instead of navigating the whole JSON tree. Agents can edit this property to help humans navigate JSON easily.

# The Markdown Analogy

What Markdown does for documents, JSON Views does for structured data: it makes an expressive, machine-friendly format comfortable for people too.

articles.title: Why we built this?
articles.body:
We needed a great JSON viewer for [**Script.it**](https://script.it/), a file-based workflow product we are building. Workflow blocks often produce JSON because it's a great format for structured data, but a wall of braces is not always a great interface, and makes it hard to validate the blocks.

We wanted people to inspect those files comfortably, and we wanted agents to help them navigate to the useful parts.

Putting a small `$jsonviews` property inside the JSON makes that straightforward. An agent can write the view settings directly into a file—or into the Python code that generates it. The next time the file opens, its pages, tables, and boards come with it.

articles.title: How the Editor Works
articles.body:
json-views render JSON files as **tables, Kanban or html views**.

### Views and schemas

The **`$jsonviews`** property saves the interface settings inside the JSON file. **Views** choose which part of the data to show and how to display it. **Schemas** describe the columns and their types, such as text, dates, or select options. You can have several views of the same data.

When these settings are absent, the editor infers useful views and field types from the data.

### Records

Each row or card represents a **record**: an item with structured properties, such as a task with a title, status, and due date. Open a record to see and edit its properties. A body property can display longer content as a document.

### Tables inside records

A record can also have a column that contains another table. For example, a project can contain milestones, and each milestone can contain checks. Click a nested collection to browse and edit its records, then return to the parent. Everything stays nested in the same JSON file.

Try **Examples → Nested JSON** to explore this.

### HTML views

Turn JSON into an editable interface with HTML and CSS. Try **Templates → Task Management → Project dashboard**.

**Templates → App Views:** [Gmail](#/files/Templates%2FApp%20Views%2FGmail%20Message.json), [HubSpot](#/files/Templates%2FApp%20Views%2FHubSpot%20Contacts.json), [Slack](#/files/Templates%2FApp%20Views%2FSlack%20Channel.json), [Notion](#/files/Templates%2FApp%20Views%2FNotion%20Project.json), [Stripe](#/files/Templates%2FApp%20Views%2FStripe%20Payments.json), [LinkedIn mock](#/files/Templates%2FApp%20Views%2FLinkedIn%20Messages%20%28Mock%29.json).

These use sample data; edits stay in the file. [API notes](./representative-examples/Templates/App%20Views/README.md) · [Build an HTML view](https://github.com/script-it/json-views/blob/main/skills/json-views/references/html-views.md).

articles.title: The file schema
Multiple ways to use json-views
articles.body:
There are two ways to use JSON Views.

### 1. Use this website

Open JSON and CSV files or folders directly in your browser. Your files are read and edited on your own machine and are never uploaded to a server. Choose a view, edit your data, then download a copy or share a snapshot link. Imported files are cached in this browser.

### 2. Build from source and use the CLI

Clone the [open-source repository](https://github.com/script-it/json-views), run `npm ci` and `npm run build`, then open a local file:

```sh
node packages/cli/bin/json-views.js ./data.json
```

The CLI runs the viewer locally and saves accepted edits back to the file. It also gives your agent a local API to work with the same document.

### Work with your agent

Use the **Agent Guide** on this website, or give your agent the [JSON Views skill](https://github.com/script-it/json-views/tree/main/skills/json-views). Ask it to organize data, add views, or help you navigate a file. You and your agent work with the same JSON and its view settings.

The website is client-only: files are read and edited in your browser. Imported documents are cached here and can return after a reload. Download a copy to keep your work beyond browser storage.

Share puts a snapshot of one file in the link itself. Anyone with the link can open their own copy; later edits do not sync. Large files can be shared as downloads instead.

No backend server stores your shared files. We use minimal anonymous usage statistics to improve the app - you can disable them in Settings.
articles.title: A very private web app
Embed json-views in your app
articles.body:
JSON Views can be embedded directly in other apps—the same way it is embedded in [Script.it](https://script.it/) to display and edit JSON produced by workflow blocks.

Use the **React component** to give your users pages, tables, boards, and a source editor inside your own interface. Pass it JSON; the data and its `$jsonviews` settings determine what appears.

**Your app owns the files and saving.** Connect a save callback to let users edit, or leave it out for a read-only viewer. You control storage, permissions, and how changes reach your agents or workflows.

See the [React integration guide](https://github.com/script-it/json-views/blob/main/packages/react/README.md#react-integration) to get started.
